title: The Crane That Lifts Stones
synopsis: Jeong Yak-yong's lifting machine will not lift a stone.
A note with a small water drop is tied to its rope.
goal: Find out if the lifting machine is broken, and who wrote the warning.

notes: Gwak's log, written out of time order with until / after: the wall's start (1794, fact h1) is fixed first and this morning's failure last; the machine worked until the carpenter came, and the note was tied in the night after his work. The rice card is not part of it. Cards and log lines are never listed in the answer's order.
One order only: lift before copy (until), copy before note (after).

learning.objective: 곽 십장의 작업 일지에서 until, after를 읽고 일이 일어난 순서를 놓아, 기계가 고장 난 것이 아니라 바뀐 것임을 알아낸다.

play.title: Broken, or Changed?
story: A big stone lies under the machine. Its ropes hang loose.
A note with a small water drop is tied to the rope.
Jeong reads its King's letters out: "The drawing is different."
play.letter:
This morning, the machine could not lift a stone.
The note was tied to the rope in the night, after the carpenter's work.
The machine lifted big stones every day, until the new carpenter came.
The King's builders began the wall in 1794.
The new carpenter rebuilt the top from a copied drawing.
play.question: Put the log in order. Was the machine broken, or changed?
hints: Look for 'until' and 'after' in the log. The lines are not in order.
What happened before the new carpenter came? What came after his work?
play.successMessage: The machine worked until someone changed it!
transition: The machine is not broken. It was changed.
Gwak says, "Nobody works here at night. The gate is shut. Only the water carriers come in before dawn."
"A copied drawing?" says Jeong. "Then which drawing is mine?"
play.orderFeedback: Read the log again. What happened until the new carpenter came?

clue.title: Changed, Not Broken
clue.note: The machine worked until a new carpenter rebuilt its top from a copied drawing.

lines.text: My machine lifts heavy stones with ropes and pulleys.
Gwak says it is broken. I do not believe it.
Then let us read his log.

discovery.detail: Someone knew the drawing was different, and tied this note in the night. Who?

play.title: Which Drawing Is Mine?
story: Three drawings of lifting machines lie on the table. Each has a name written on it.
The new carpenter stands by the door. "I cannot read. I took the drawing with a gate on it."
"Only three people come in here," Jeong says. "The carpenter, my clerk, and the girl who brings water for my ink."
"Read my words, and find my drawing."
play.letter:
"My machine stands like a gate, with a beam across the top."
"Pulleys hang from the beam. More pulleys hang under them, over the stone."
"Ropes run between the pulleys, up and down."
"A big wheel stands on each side. Workers turn the wheels."
play.question: Which drawing is Jeong's?
hints: Read Jeong's first line. What shape does his machine have?
Look for pulleys in two places, and a wheel on each side.
transition: The machine in the yard has pulleys only at the top, and no wheels.
"He took the gate with no wheels," says Jeong. "Let us rebuild it, and lift that stone."

clue.title: Jeong's Drawing
clue.value: PULLEYS ABOVE AND BELOW, A WHEEL ON EACH SIDE
clue.note: Jeong's machine is like a gate, with pulleys in two places and two wheels. Only the carpenter, the clerk and the water girl come into the drawing room.

evidence.name: Jeong's Drawing
evidence.description: A frame like a gate. Pulleys under the beam and over the stone. A wheel on each side.

options.label: Tie the ropes around the stone
Push the stone up a slope
Hook the stone to the lower pulleys

notes: Jeong's steps (made up) are written out of order with before / after / last: tie before hook, turn after hook, rise last. Two decoys (pull by hand, push up a slope) are what nobody does.

clueInputs.note: The machine is rebuilt from Jeong's drawing.

learning.objective: 정약용의 순서 설명(before, only after, last)을 읽고 돌을 들어 올리는 네 단계를 차례대로 고른다.
expressions: Before you hook the stone, tie the ropes around it.
only after the stone is hooked

play.title: The Stone Rises
story: The builders rebuild the machine from Jeong's drawing.
Now the big stone must go up onto the wall.
"Read my steps," says Jeong. "Then do them in order."
play.letter:
"Turn the two wheels only after the stone is hooked."
"Before you hook the stone, tie the ropes around it."
"The stone rises last."
"Nobody pulls the rope by hand, and nobody pushes the stone."
play.question: Tap the four steps in order.
hints: Find the step that comes before the hook.
The wheels turn only after the hook. What happens last?
play.successMessage: The wheels turn, and the stone rises!
transition: The ropes go tight. Slowly, the big stone rises onto the wall.
Gwak takes off his hat. "It was never broken," he says.
Below, a girl with a water bucket looks at the two wheels, and smiles.

feedback.hook,tie,turn,rise: Read again: what do you do before you hook the stone?
feedback.tie,turn,hook,rise: The wheels turn only after the stone is hooked.

play.orderFeedback: Those are the right steps. Read Jeong's 'before' and 'after' again.

clue.title: The Stone Rises
clue.note: Rebuilt from Jeong's drawing, the machine lifts the stone onto the wall.

evidence.name: Jeong's Lifting Steps
evidence.description: Tie the ropes, hook the stone, turn the two wheels, and the stone rises.

options.feedback: The clerk sleeps in town, and the gate is shut at night. The note came in the night.

options.feedback: Gwak never goes into the drawing room. How could he know the drawing was different?

options.label: The new carpenter

notes: Who tied the note (made up): three conditions read from the case: the writer saw Jeong's drawing (the drawing room: carpenter, clerk, water girl; Gwak never goes in), can write (the carpenter cannot), and was in the yard at night (the gate is shut; the clerk sleeps in town; only the water carriers come before dawn). Only Okbun fits all three. The water drop is never needed to choose: its meaning is told in the ending. Options are listed so the answer is not first.

clueInputs.note: The note was tied in the night, after the carpenter's work.
Only the carpenter, the clerk and the water girl come into the drawing room.
The stone is on the wall: the machine works again.

play.title: Who Tied the Note?
story: The big stone sits on the wall. The workers cheer.
Jeong holds up the note. "Someone warned us. Who?"
Four people stand in the yard.
play.letterIntro: Your notebook, and what the four people say:
play.letter:
The note says: "The drawing is different."
It is written in the King's letters.
It was tied to the rope in the night.
Gwak: "I never go into the drawing room."
The carpenter: "I cannot read or write."
The clerk: "I sleep in town. The yard gate is shut at night."
Okbun: "I take water to the drawing room. I fill the jars before dawn."
play.question: Who tied the note to the rope?
hints: To write "the drawing is different", the writer had seen Jeong's drawing.
Check each person: the drawing room, the writing, the night. Only one fits all three.
play.successMessage: Okbun! Only she fits all three.
transition: "I saw the new top had no wheels," she says. "Jeong's drawing has two."

evidence.name: The Finished Fortress
evidence.description: Okbun, a water girl at the yard, wrote the warning note. Hwaseong was finished in 1796. Machines like the geojunggi helped lift big stones. A record book lists the workers and their pay.

ending.text: The new top had no wheels. Jeong's drawing has two. So I wrote the note.
ending.speaker: okbun

ending.text: Why a water drop, and no name?
A water girl may not tell the builders they are wrong. So I wrote no name.
ending.speaker: okbun

ending.text: I drew a water drop. Jeong knows the girl who brings his water.
ending.speaker: okbun

ending.speaker: okbun

Machines like mine helped lift the big stones.

hook: A stone waits under a machine that will not lift.

learningGoal.title: Reading order words and how a machine is made

objectives: Put the work log in order.
Lift the stone in the right order.
Find who tied the note to the rope.
intro: Spring, 1795. You are a detective, a guest of Jeong Yak-yong at Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon.
A long stone wall is rising around the new town.
Jeong planned this fortress for the King. He also designed a lifting machine, the geojunggi.
It lifts heavy stones with ropes and pulleys. Today Jeong has come to see it work.
But Foreman Gwak shouts across the stone yard.
"Your machine is broken! It cannot lift one stone!"
play.caseSummary: The lifting machine was not broken. A new carpenter, who could not read, rebuilt its top from the wrong drawing. Okbun, who carries water to the builders, had seen Jeong's drawing. She tied a warning note to the rope in the night. It had a water drop and no name. Rebuilt from Jeong Yak-yong's drawing, the machine lifted the stone. Hwaseong Fortress was finished in 1796. Machines like Jeong's geojunggi helped lift big stones. A record book lists the workers and their pay.

notes: PART 10 (2026-11-06), Case 03. Jeong Yak-yong is real; his words here are made up. Foreman Gwak, the new carpenter, the clerk and Okbun are made up; so are the stopped machine, the copied drawing, the three drawings and the record chest.

PART 2 (2026-11-09): the final is a text choice: who tied the note (Okbun), found by three conditions (saw Jeong's drawing, can write, in the yard at night). The ending still tells 1796 (h1), the machines (h2, h3) and the record of workers and pay (h4, h5); Jeong planned the fortress (h8) and Jo Sim-tae ran the site (h7).
